documentation.range:
The distribution of the Black Caiman encompasses much of northern and central South America, including seven countries: Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, French Guiana, Guyana, and Peru, but more than 70% of its distribution area falls within Brazil. The presence of the species in Venezuela has been refuted several times.

Widely and exclusively distributed throughout the Amazon region, the Black Caiman’s distribution includes the Andean-Amazonian piedmont in the northwest, Amazon floodplain forests, and tributaries of the Amazon River that flow from the Brazilian and Guiana Shields, as well as coastal regions in French Guiana. It occurs in a diversity of environments throughout its distribution, occupying large rivers and canals, oxbow lakes, flooded grasslands, floating meadows, and wetlands associated with Amazonian swamps and peatlands. It also occurs in flooded savannas and environments associated with coastal mangroves and wet coastal savannas. However, it is more abundant in waterbodies in the Amazonian ﬂoodplain forests (Medem 1963, 1981, 1983; Plotkin et al. 1983a; Vasquez 1991; Ross 1998; Da Silveira 2002; Thorbjarnarson 2010; Campos et al. 2018).
documentation.population:
Melanosuchus niger is widely distributed throughout the Amazon region, embracing much of northern and central South America and occupying various habitats, including large rivers, flooded areas, swamps and river meanders. The effect of commercial hunting, mainly for the skin trade in the mid-20th century and for the meat trade at the end of the 1970s, resulted in an evident decline in the wild populations. Although there are few population studies of M. niger, and its abundance is not homogeneous throughout its distribution, reports show the recovery of its original distribution in some areas, with high-density populations indicating that M. niger is apparently an abundant species, only partially and locally depleted (Rebêlo and Magnusson 1983; Yamashita et al. 1996; Da Silveira and Thorbjarnarson 1999; Da Silveira 2002, 2003; Farias et al. 2004; Vasconcelos 2005; De Thoisy et al. 2006; Da Silveira et al. 2008, 2011; Thorbjarnarson 2010; Botero-Arias and Regatieri 2013; Marioni et al. 2013a, 2021; Botero-Arias et al. 2022).

Population studies of M. niger have demonstrated genetic structure based on mitochondrial markers and microsatellites. There is evidence of genetic differentiation between populations in the northeast distribution in French Guiana and the State of Amapá (Brazil), compared to those in Ecuador and western Brazilian Amazonia (Farias et al. 2004, Vasconcelos 2005, De Thoisy et al. 2006, Vasconcelos et al. 2008). With the utilization of different markers (Cytochrome B and SNPs) and expanding the number of samples, it was discovered that the genetic structure of M. niger populations is strongly linked to different factors such as isolation by distance, presence of waterfalls and rapids, and distinct watersheds. This information enabled the identification of at least eight Management Units with particular relevance for the conservation of the species (Hernández-Rangel 2015, Hernández-Rangel et al. 2022; Hernández-Rangel et al. unpublished data).

BoliviaMelanosuchus niger is classified as Vulnerable (VU) on Bolivia's National Red List (2008) (Llobet et al. 2008). It mainly inhabits the northeast of the country, specifically in the departments of Beni, Cochabamba, La Paz, Pando, and Santa Cruz. The species is particularly prevalent in protected areas within these departments, such as Noel Kempff Mercado National Park, Madidi National Park, Isiboro Sécure Indigenous Territory and National Park, Amazonica Manuripi National Reserve, Pilón Lajas Biosphere Reserve, and Beni Biological Station Biosphere Reserve. The species in Bolivia has experienced slow recovery rates in most of its historical distribution, and low population densities continue to be a concern throughout its range (King and Videz-Roca 1989, Pacheco 1993, Ten et al. 2008, Rodriguez-Cordero 2019, Rodriguez-Cordero et al. 2019). Intense hunting for its skins between the 1940s to 1960s resulted in a significant decline in the natural populations of M. niger (Plotkin et al. 1983a).

In the 2000s, population studies were carried out in 12 lakes in the Ichilo River floodplain (department of Santa Cruz) and the average observed density of M. niger was one individual/km. It was also reported that small M. niger populations, consisting mainly of sub-adults and juveniles, were found in the Bolivian Amazon Basin (Aguilera et al. 2008), although it occurs in fewer water bodies than Caiman yacare, which is sympatric in its range. In the Low Ichoa River Basin, Isidoro Securé National Park (department of Beni), M. niger were recorded at observed densities of 1.6 to 2.2 individual/km (Mendez 2006, Rodriguez-Cordero 2019). In Baures TUIOC (Autonomous and communally owned indigenous land, department of Beni), 19% of the population was confirmed as M. niger whilst the remainder were C. yacare (Chungara 2017). Also, in the department of Beni, surveys of the Joaquiniano TUIOC recorded 255 M. niger at an observed density of 1.93 individuals/km, mainly sub-adults [total length (TL) between 51 and 120 cm], with the highest densities recorded in forest lakes (Pallete 2015, Rodriguez-Cordero 2019).

Between 2015 and 2017, surveys were conducted during the dry season on the floodplains of the Beni basin, including the Mamoré, Iténez, and Beni sub-basins. The surveys covered 1,507 km of shoreline and registered a total of 53,551 individuals, of which only 2,854 (5.33%) were M. niger. The surveys were carried out on nine Indigenous Lands, and the abundance of M. niger varied among waterbodies types: Baure ranged from 0.82 to 29 individuals/km, Canichana from 0.68 to 3.95 individuals/km, Cayubaba from 1.40 to 27.50 individuals/km, Itonama from 2.50 to 23.15 individuals/km, Joaquiniano from 2.37 to 32.70 individuals/km, Moré from 1.82 to 8.86 individuals/km, Movima from 1.04 to 27.92 individuals/km, Sirionó from 0.00 to 0.8 individuals/km and Tacana from 1.43 to 105.0 individuals/km. The study showed significant differences in the abundance of M. niger in the waterbodies occupied, with a population structure dominated by juveniles and sub-adults (TL between 81 and 180 cm), indicating a slow population recovery (Rivas et al. 2023).

Recent surveys conducted between 2020 and 2021 in eight lowland management areas in the departments of Beni and Santa Cruz found small populations of, again, mainly juvenile and sub-adult M. niger, with densities ranging from 0.35 to 8.13 individuals/km (mean 3.7 individuals/km). The Itenéz Integrated Management Natural Area Departmental Park (River Itenéz) and the Baures and Cavineno TUIOC had the highest densities (Rios 2022).

Brazil:The latest update of the Brazilian Red List reports that Melanosuchus niger is currently considered a species of Least Concern (LC), with stable populations and likely an upward trend (Marioni et al. 2013b, Coutinho et al. 2022). The species is widely distributed across an extensive part of the Brazilian territory, representing almost 70% of the total range of the species. In Brazil, M. niger can be found in the Amazon, Tocantins, and Araguaia basins, as well as in rivers located in the State of Amapá that flow directly into the Atlantic Ocean. However, population density varies among regions. Various studies have been conducted to evaluate this variation, and high densities have been recorded in some locations (Marioni et al. 2013a, Silva et al. 2021, Coutinho et al. 2022).

A study conducted by Da Silveira (2002) in the Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve (State of Amazonas) revealed a 580% increase in the number of M. niger seen, from 556 individuals in 1994 to 3,789 individuals in 1998. The proportion of M. niger compared to Spectacled Caiman (Caiman crocodilus) increased from 38% to 82%, and the number of nesting females increased from one nest in 1996 to 22 nests in 1999. Currently, M. niger in the Mamirauá SDR has a stable population trend, representing 85–90% of total caimans seen (the rest are predominantly C. crocodilus) and a high density of M. niger nests (Botero-Arias, unpublished data).

Between 2004 and 2005, spotlight surveys conducted in 85 locations across five Brazilian states (Amazonas, Amapá, Goiás, Rondônia, and Tocantins) detected M. niger in 94% of the locations, totalling 36,962 individuals. The density ranged from 2.1 to 466.5 individuals/km (CITES 2007). Similarly, monitoring conducted from 2004 to 2008 in the Lago do Cuniã Extractive Reserve (State of Rondônia) recorded average observed densities ranging from 5.1 to 100.4 individuals/km (Mendonça and Coutinho 2009), which remained stable over the period of study (Marioni et al. 2013a, Coutinho et al. 2022).

Surveys conducted between 2006 and 2009 in the Meandros do Rio Araguaia Environmental Protection Area (State of Tocantins) also indicate that the M. niger population has been growing in the region (Andrade and Coutinho 2007; Andrade and Coutinho 2009). Additionally, a study conducted in 2008 in the unprotected area of the Lake Badajós region (State of Amazonas), found 1,266 caimans, of which 82% were M. niger, with the density ranging from 14 to 38 individuals/km (Marioni et al. 2013a). Another study conducted in 2008 in Cabo Orange National Park, located in the northernmost region of Brazil, sampled 46.3 km of rivers and lakes and sighted 425 caimans, of which 370 (87%) were identified as M. niger (Andrade and Coutinho 2011).

Colombia:
In 2015, the National Red List classified Melanosuchus niger as Vulnerable (VU) (Morales-Betancourt and Trujillo 2015). Although there are indications of population recovery in some areas, densities remain very low. Moreover, each subpopulation is estimated to have less than 1,000 mature individuals (Morales-Betancourt and Trujillo 2015). The species is distributed in the Amazonas, Putumayo, and Vaupés departments. M. niger was once abundant throughout the Colombian Amazon region, especially in the lower Caquetá and Putumayo Rivers, the Caucayá River, and La Apaya Lake. However, commercial hunting for skins, which began in the 1930s, caused a significant decline in the wild population. By the end of the 1970s, the species was considered extinct in Colombian territory (Medem 1981, Plotkin et al. 1983a, Barahona et al. 1996a, Rodríguez-Melo 2000). Between 1994 and 1997, surveys conducted in 14 localities of the Putumayo, upper Caquetá, Caguán, Apaporis, and Amazon Rivers found the highest relative apparent densities of the caiman in La Apaya (0.64 individuals/ha), Sunicocha (0.32 individuals/ha), and Yarinas (0.29 individuals/km) in the Putumayo River basin and Garzacocha Lake (0.85 individuals/ha) in the Upper Amazon River. The reports concluded that caiman numbers were increasing, particularly in the Putumayo River (Barahona et al. 1996a, Barahona et al. 1996b, Rodríguez-Melo 2000). For the formulation of the national program for the conservation and sustainable use of M. niger, the surveys and interviews indicated that the species was present in 50% of the 139 sites visited, with a population structure typical of unexploited areas in the Putumayo River between the Santa Clara and Puerto Ticuna sectors, where adults, juveniles, and hatchlings were present. In 2008 and 2009, studies evaluated populations of M. niger in the Caquetá (La Pedrera), Putumayo (Tarapacá and Puerto Leguízamo), Amazon, and Loreto Yacu Rivers, and nearby lakes. The highest apparent densities were found in the lakes of the Putumayo River basin (Tarapacá: 0.53 individuals/km and Puerto Leguízamo: 0.38 individuals/km (Bermúdez-Romero 2010).
Ecuador:Melanosuchus niger is considered Vulnerable (VU) in the National Red List (Carrillo et al. 2005). The species is distributed in northeastern Ecuador in the provinces of Orellana and Sucumbíos, and reported in several protected areas; Yasuní National Park, Limoncocha Biological Reserve, Cuyabeno Wildlife Reserve (Reserva de Producción de Fauna) and Tiputini Biodiversity Station. Heavy hunting between 1930 and 1970 resulted in significant population reductions. However, the species has recovered slowly, despite considerable fragmentation among areas.

Most of the information on the status of M. niger in Ecuador comes from a few locations of the Aguarico River system (Cuyabeno lakes and river, Lagartococha lake system and river, Imuya Pacuya and Zancudococha lakes) and in the Napo River system (Tiputini and Yasuni Rivers, and Limoncocha, Taracoa, Añangucocha, Challuacocha, Garzacocha and Jatuncocha lakes). In the 1980s, M. niger was already common in some areas of the Ecuadorian Amazon, with significant populations in various river systems. Apparent densities for populations of the Aguarico were stable during several annual surveys in the Cuyabeno region (3.15 to 5.68 individuals/km over nine years), Zancudococha (23.5 individuals/km over five years) and Imuya (23.6 individuals/km over two years). However, the Limoncocha Lake population, belonging to the Napo system, suffered declines over eight years of annual surveys (Asanza 1992). Between 1992 and 1994, 18 surveys were conducted and M. niger were observed in almost all localities, with densities ranging from 0 to 13.5 individuals/km. The locations with the highest densities (>10 individuals/km) were Challuacocha, Imuya, and Limoncocha (Hines and Rice 1992; Hines and Rice 1994). In the mid-1990s, a long-term monitoring effort in Cuyabeno Reserve reported observed densities ranging from 0.13 to 3.41 individuals/km in several lakes within the reserve (Ron 1995, Vallejo 1995, Vallejo et al. 1996, Ron et al. 1998). In 1999, the mean density reported for some lakes in northeastern Ecuadorian Amazonia was 6.6 individuals/km, comparable to the densities previously reported in this region by Hines and Rice (1994) and Ron (1995) but lower than those reported by Asanza (1992) in Zancudococha and Imuya (Endara 2000). Continuing the surveys almost a decade later, researchers focused on five previously studied lakes: Canangueno, Mateococha, Zancudococha and Imuya. The results showed apparent densities of up to 8.89 individuals/km and a higher proportion of M. niger than Caiman crocodilus in the latter two lakes (Dueñas-Serrano 2008). In 2012, the number of M. niger were recorded for two Cuyabeno lakes, Canangueno and Mateococha, which revealed a consistently low density and species proportion compared to data collected over 17 years (Ortiz 2012, Ortiz et al. 2020). Between 2002 and 2011, monitoring in Limoncocha reported apparent densities of up to 8.73 individuals/km. These results suggest that the population has remained stable during these years (Thorbjarnarson 2003, Urresta 2003, Villamarin 2006, Carrillo 2009, Madera 2011). In 2017, the most recent survey of caimans was conducted to standardize a monitoring protocol for M. niger in four different areas: Huririma, Salado, and Lagaro Rivers and Jatuncocha Lake. The survey reported an encounter rate ranging from 0 to 5.7 individuals/km (Naveda-Rodríguez et al. 2020).

French Guiana:Melanosuchus niger is classified as Near Threatened (NT) on the National Red List (La Liste Rouge des Espèces Menacées en France, Faune Vertébrée de Guyane; Moncorps et al. 2017). The species has been protected by Ministerial decree since 1986 and almost 50% of its current distribution area is within the designated Kaw-Roura Nature Reserve with a RAMSAR classification. Melanosuchus niger is limited to the northeast corner of French Guiana, inhabiting the mangroves and seasonally flooded grasslands of Kaw River, the swampy area of Savanne Angélique, the mangroves of the lower part of the Approuague River (Plotkin et al. 1983a,b), although there haven’t been any confirmed sightings in several years, and Pointe Béhague (De Thoisy and Auffret 2003). While the species was previously found in the Mahury and Oyak Rivers in the west, and the Kourouai and Ouanary Rivers in the east, it became extinct in those areas due to commercial hunting (De Thoisy and Auffret 2003). The first study of M. niger in the Kaw region was conducted in 1979, revealing a high density of the species and the presence of some large individuals (Darlington 1979, Plotkin et al. 1983b). Later expeditions to the Angelique and Gabrielle Creeks in the same region found high densities (up to 38 and 48 individuals/km, respectively) mainly in inaccessible areas, in contrast with dramatic population declines at the edges (Ouboter et al. 1999, Blanc and De Thoisy 2001). A recent survey in Agami Pond, one of the Kaw marshes areas that holds water during the dry season, confirmed the presence of a large M. niger population, with most individuals measuring up to 2 metres (Caut et al. 2019).

An ongoing mark-recapture study by Lemaire and Mangione (unpublished data) has collected data on M. niger since 2019 in two locations in Kaw-Roura Nature Reserve, namely the Kaw River and Savanne Angélique, a swamp area with several permanent water bodies and patches of flooded forest. Compared to the high abundance of Caiman crocodilus and Paleosuchus palpebrosus in the Kaw Rriver, M. niger density is low, which might be explained by continuous illegal harvest. The inaccessible Savanne Angélique site has a high density of sub-adult and adult individuals, with a further increase of adults during the breeding season of migratory Agami Herons (Agamia agami) from mid-April until end of June. During this time, occurrence of individuals greater than 4 m temporarily increases (R. Mangione, unpublished data). Nevertheless, most of French Guiana’s M. niger habitat is inaccessible, and so far no hatchlings have been observed in the principal locations, indicating the seclusion of breeding areas.

Guyana:
Guyana law protects Melanosuchus niger, which is classified as a "Totally Protected Species" under the Wildlife Conservation and Management Act of 2016. The distribution of M. niger in Guyana is restricted to the upper and middle Essequibo, Rupununi, Rewa and Berbice Rivers, as well as the Takatu and Ireng Rivers in the Amazon basin (Medem 1983, Plotkin et al. 1983a, Gorzula et al. 1990). However, commercial hunting in the 1950s caused significant depletion of the natural populations, and the species was almost extinct by 1965 (Medem 1983, Gorzula et al. 1990, Uruena 1990, Spellen 2019). Recent studies have shown a recovery in the population of M. niger (Spellen 2019, 2020).
Gorzula and Woolford (1990) reported the species in 16 localities in Guyana, with a notable recovery in the northern Rupununi region. They reported a density of 7.4 individuals/km over 41.2 km of shoreline surveyed and estimated the population to be between 2,000 and 4,000 non-hatchlings. This population was considered one of the largest in South America (Uruena 1990). The recovery of the species continued through the 1990s, and reports in the 2000s indicated that populations in North Rupununi Wetlands were abundant (J.B. Thorbjarnarson, pers. comm., 2010). Watkins (2002) observed 2,443 individuals in 300 km of river and 275 km of lakes in the Rupununi, Rewa and Essequibo basins, with an density of non-hatchling caimans of 1.82 individuals/km in rivers and 4.18 individuals/km in lakes. Taylor (2006) and Spellen (2019) also reported a healthy population in the Rupununi River, with encounter rates up to 16.9 individuals/km during the low water period. Ingwall-King (2013) estimated a density of 3.1 individuals/km in a small section of the Rewa River. The most recent survey of M. niger populations in Guyana, conducted in the Rupununi, Rewa and Essequibo Rivers, observed 1,609 caimans in 184.5 km of sections, with mean encounter rates of 11.99, 8.89, and 14.54 individuals/km, respectively (Spellen 2019, 2020). There is a well-studied and recovering population of M. niger in Yupukari, located on the Rupununi River. The Caiman House Field Station (CHFS) serves as a base of operations for a long-term mark-recapture study of the local population since 2005, with over 750 marked individuals. The community also operates ecotourism activities, providing access to large adult M. niger (Rosenblatt et al. 2021).

Peru:
Melanosuchus niger is classified as Near Threatened (NT) in the Peruvian Red List (SERFOR 2018). The species is found in the Amazonian lowland forests of the northeast and east of the country, including the Loreto, Ucayali, Madre de Dios, San Martín, and Huánuco departments. The species was once abundant in Peru, but commercial hunting led to a decline in wild populations, which were rare in the 1970s and 1980s, and considered on the border of extinction (Plotkin et al. 1983a).
In the southern region of Peru, population studies were conducted in Cocha Cashu in Manú National Park from 1971 to 1972, which showed a population size of 37 individuals, mostly juveniles (Otte 1978). In 1977, there was a 50-60% increase in population size and by 1982, the population was estimated to be 213 individuals (Vásquez 1982). In Cocha Cashu, an apparent density was reported of 24.74 to 27.75 individuals/km, with a population skewed heavily towards juveniles (Herron 1985). Although M. niger is now widespread in this region, and has shown clear signs of recovery, they are not highly abundant in most areas.

Surveys at the Pacaya National Reserve between 1967 and 1968 registered apparent densities of M. niger up to 2 individuals/km, with a ratio of 1:20 relative to Caiman crocodilus (Ponce and Hofmann 1968). Twelve years later, surveys in the Samiria River in Pacaya-Samiria National Reserve registered a mean observed density of 0.28 individuals/km, with a proportion of 1:30.4 to C. crocodilus (Verdi et al. 1980). In the Jenaro Herrera region, a density of 0.46 individuals/km was reported in the lake system at the beginning of the 1970s. In 1978, the apparent density was 3.11 individuals/ha in nearby swamp areas (Ríos et al. 1974, Vásquez 1981). In the Samiria River basin, overall encounter rates between 0.52 and 1.14 individuals/km have been reported (Street 2003). An evaluation in the Samiria River basin showed variation in the abundance of M. niger among areas according to hunting level, with intensive hunting (Shiringal) showing 0.13 individuals/km, moderate hunting (Tacshacocha and Ungurahui) showing 1.6 and 1.41 individuals/km, and a low hunting area (Santa Elena) showing 0.51 individuals/km (Bodmer et al. 2005). In 2007, evaluations in the Pacaya and Yanayacu Pucate River basins found a mean M. niger encounter rate of 2.32 individuals/km, with the highest density for the Pacaya basin where 5.38 individuals/km and for the Yanayacu basin where up to 17.19 individuals/km were seen in some areas (ProNaturaleza 2007). Between 2012 and 2016, the observed abundance of M. niger in Pacaya Samiria National Reserve varied in different sectors: Tacshacocha ranged from 0.04 to 1.09 individuals/km, Ungurahui from 0.03 to 8.14 individuals/km, Wishto from 0.08 to 5.97 individuals/km, Pithecia from 0.88 to 4.1 individuals/km and Santa Elena were at 0.75 individuals/km. In 2014, only one M. niger was observed in Pucacuro National Park (J.D. Freitas, pers. comm., 2017).

Studies conducted in the Yavarí River basin, on the border between Peru and Brazil, showed that out of the total caimans observed, nine were M. niger, 10 were Paleosuchus trigonatus and 463 were Caiman crocodilus (Newell, 2001). In the Lago Preto region of the Yavarí River, a total of 540 caimans were reported, with only 24 being M. niger and an apparent density of 0.32 individuals/km (Swan 2005). Freezer (2008) recorded 720 caimans, of which only 13 were M. niger, at an apparent density of 0.18 individuals/km. Bodmer et al. (2009) reported an apparent density in Lago Preto of 0.34 individuals/km, a slight non-significant increasing trend in M. niger numbers seen between 2001 and 2008. In the Yavarí-Mirín, Pérez-Peña et al. (2012) reported a M. niger apparent density of 0.22 individuals/km.
documentation.habitats:
Melanosuchus niger, as the largest Amazonian predator, is considered a keystone species, playing an important role in the trophic network (Fittkau 1970, Somaweera et al. 2020, Griffith et al. 2022, Lourenço-de-Moraes et al. 2023). The species can occupy a wide variety of environments in rural and urban areas, including artificial waterbodies resulting from hydropower dams, artificial lakes, and water reservoirs (Marioni et al. 2013a, 2021b; Campos et al. 2018). However, the species is absent in small forest streams and streamlets of closed-canopy terra firme forests (upland forest), especially near the headwaters, with low incident sunlight. The species is rare or absent upstream of rapids and waterfalls. Although M. niger is found in habitats where it overlaps with other caiman species, several authors have suggested they seem to have a different niche.

Melanosuchus niger is the biggest Amazonian vertebrate and the largest of the seven Alligatoridae species. However, the maximum size of both sexes is difficult to determine. Medem (1983) cited hunted individuals that surpassed 5.1 m total length (TL). Studies in Guyana reported that size-at-age models predicted that males and females reach mean asymptotic sizes of 3.8 m and 2.9 m TL, respectively (Taylor et al. 2016). In Brazil, information available on somatic growth indicated that small to medium-sized individuals grow more slowly in floodplain forest (várzea) habitats with high primary productivity and a high caiman abundance in comparison with the blackwater-flooded forests (igapó) habitat with lower productivity and low caiman abundance, indicating a density-dependent process (Da Silveira et al. 2013).

Age and size at maturity are also unknown for both sexes. Histological analysis of gonads and bones in two wild males (1.8 m and 2.9 m TL, respectively) indicated the former was still immature and the latter an adult, at estimated ages of 10 and 14 years, respectively. Similarly, histology of the reproductive systems of two females (2.2 m and 2.9 m TL, respectively) were reportedly immature and reproductively capable, respectively, at around 15 and 17 years of age (Da Silveira et al., unpublished data). Without accurate empirical support, several authors have assumed that females start nesting at 2.5 m TL, meaning an age of 19 to 20 years in the Brazil study (Da Silveira et al. 2013) and 13.7 to 22.8 years in the Guyana study (Taylor et al. 2016). Age at maturity estimation in males is more complex. Even if they are physiologically capable of reproduction, small males may be inhibited from mating by larger individuals. Multiple paternity (polyandry) has been reported for a small caiman population in Anavilhanas National Park in the Brazilian Central Amazon (Muniz et al. 2011).

This species builds mound nests during the dry season, in forests, near banks or on masses of floating aquatic plants, locally known as matupá. Females generally lay between 35 and 50 eggs. Eggs have a rigid shell and an elliptical shape, weighing 121.8 g on average (Medem 1963, 1981, 1983; Villamarín-Jurado and Suárez 2007; Thorbjarnarson 2010; Villamarín et al. 2011, 2021; Barão-Nóbrega et al. 2018; Silva et al. 2021).

Melanosuchus niger populations are widely dispersed in available habitats during the flooding season. In the dry season, they concentrate in permanent lakes, rivers, canals and riverbeds, exhibiting gregarious behaviour in juveniles and sub-adults. The large adults probably hold territories, increasing competition for food, high-quality nesting sites and potential partners (Plotkin et al. 1983a; Thorbjarnarson 1998, 2010; Da Silveira et al. 2008; Caut et al. 2019).

Melanosuchus niger show seasonal movements in response to changes in water levels, prey availability and population density (Caut et al. 2019). Like other crocodilians, M. niger is considered a territorial species, with dominant males having a defined home range which they patrol and defend within broad movement patterns. Females appear to use a well-defined zone, associated with nesting areas and a small home range, restricted to brief seasonal movements. Juveniles may disperse from their natal areas in search of new habitats. In some cases, they may undertake long-distance movements (Da Silveira et al. 2011a). An unexpected long movement was reported for a male (3.6 m TL) using VHF radio-tracking in the Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve. The individual was killed four years and seven months after the initial measurement for the salt-meat trade in the Amana SDR, 33 km from the capture site. This long movement may indicate the size of reserves that may be required to protect the species (Da Silveira et al. 2011a).
documentation.threats:
Melanosuchus niger was abundant in the 19th century. However, due to the high profitability of the skin trade, intense hunting began in the 1900s and continued, although less intensively, through the 1970s. This overexploitation was identified as a contributing factor to the decline of wild M. niger populations (Medem 1981, 1983; Plotkin et al. 1983a; Brazaitis et al. 1996; Da Silveira and Thorbjarnarson 1999; Thorbjarnarson 1999; Thorbjarnarson 2010; Thorbjarnarson and Da Silveira 2000; Antunes et al. 2016; Botero-Arias et al. 2022).

Prior to the 1990s, M. niger was categorized as one of the most endangered crocodilian species in the Neotropical region (Medem 1981, 1983; Plotkin et al. 1983a). The primary factors contributing to their endangerment were unsustainable practices, such as trading their skin, as well as habitat loss and degradation caused by human activities. Additionally, local fishermen hunted them due to perceived competition for resources. In over half of the countries where this species can be found, wild populations were considered severely depleted (Medem 1981, Brazaitis et al. 1996, Yamashita et al. 1996, Ross 1998, Da Silveira and Thorbjarnarson 1999, Da Silveira 2002, Vasconcelos 2005, Rueda-Almonacid et al. 2007, Botero-Arias et al. 2010, Botero-Arias et al. 2014, Mendonça et al. 2016, Marioni et al. 2021, Botero-Arias et al. 2022, Esbach et al. 2022).

Following the prohibition of M. niger hunting in the 1970s, the exportation of their skins declined significantly. There had been no recorded cases of regional or international trade in caiman skins since the 1980s (Rebêlo and Magnusson 1983, Brazaitis et al. 1996, Marioni et al. 2021, Botero-Arias et al. 2022). Nevertheless, the trade of caiman meat emerged as an unlawful substitute as an income source for local people. In the 1980s, the Middle Amazon River (called the Solimões River in Brazil) became a major global hub for the illicit trade of caiman meat, traded mainly to Colombia and Pará State in Brazil, and often sold as salted pirarucu meat (Arapaima gigas) (Da Silveira and Thorbjarnarson 1999). However, implementing the Mamiraua SDR and a community-based resource management system helped reduced the illegal caiman trade. It was eventually replaced by the Piagaçu-Purus SDR on the lower Purus River, which became a significant hub for the trade of salted caiman meat in the 2000s, sold mostly in a little-known market in the state of Pará, Brazil (Da Silveira and Thorbjarnarson 1999, Marioni et al. 2007, Mendonça et al. 2016).

The M. niger meat trade appears to have diminished around the Amazon on both the local and regional scales. However, the informal trade of salted meat is considered an important activity that could affect local caiman populations. Nonetheless, there have been indications of recovery in several areas where populations have increased despite continued sporadic hunting.

The use of M. niger and Amazonian dolphins as bait for the piracatinga fishing activities is currently considered the most significant threat. Although the efforts of conservationists, community scientists, environmental agencies and society moved to ban the piracatinga trade and the illegal use of caiman and dolphins, the magnitude and effect of this activity still needs to be evaluated (Da Silveira and Viana 2003, Botero-Arias et al. 2014, Brum et al. 2015, Franco et al. 2016, Pimenta et al. 2018, Marioni et al. 2021).

The rise in M. niger abundance has resulted in an increased frequency of human-crocodile conflict over the last decade, including some fatalities, as well as attacks on domestic animals and pets. This has resulted in a negative perception of caiman, leading to the pre-emptive removal of several caimans in an attempt to avoid potential confrontations and prevent future attacks. With the urban expansion and changes in the annual flooding regime (more extreme water levels), negative interactions between M. niger and humans are becoming increasingly common in closer proximity to cities and human settlements (Cook et al. 2022, Haddad Jr et al. 2011, Hernández-Rangel et al. 2010, Pierre et al. 2023). This has been particularly evident through frequent reports on social media. Moreover, there have been reports of the destruction of caiman nests and the killing of hatchlings by local people in an attempt to control the growth of wild caiman populations (T.A. Andrade, pers. comm. 2011).

Additionally, with the increase in densities, M. niger are occasionally killed due to the misconception that caimans compete with human fishers and cause economic losses due to fishing equipment damaged by caimans. Further, the expanded use of various fishing methods, such as hooks, nets, and traps, aimed at capturing commercial fish, such as pirarucu (Arapaima gigas), has led to caimans becoming trapped and drowning (Rueda-Almonacid et al. 2007, Alonso et al. 2008, Hernández-Rangel et al. 2010, Cook et al. 2022, Harris et al. 2022, Pierre et al. 2023).

Populations of M. niger are likely affected by urban expansion, logging, and other forms of habitat destruction. Deforestation and burning of riversides for harbour construction, community crops and buffalo breeding can cause degradation, erosion and loss of habitat, leading to the destruction of vegetation in riparian areas, which can negatively impact wild populations (Plotkin et al. 1983a, Hernández-Rangel et al. 2010, Marioni et al. 2013a, Botero-Arias et al. 2022). The transformation of the habitat for the construction of dams and hydroelectric reservoirs has suggested a strong effect on the population dynamic, behaviour, and biology of M. niger. Campos (2015) documented the death of 42 caimans in the Santo Antônio dam reservoir area over a two-year period, with more than half measuring over 4 m TL. The damming of rivers causes flooding in these areas, bringing caimans and fishermen into closer proximity, which can exacerbate conflicts, particularly with larger individuals.

Studies have shown that caimans are affected by bioaccumulation in their tissues through the trophic chain, particularly by mercury (Hg). This occurs through biomagnification in the food chain of aquatic organisms, which can have harmful effects on wildlife and pose potential health risks to humans (Brazaitis et al. 1996; Schneider et al. 2012; Schneider et al. 2015; Eggins et al. 2015; Marrugo-Negrete et al. 2019; Lemaire et al. 2021a,b,c, 2022). Illegal gold exploration and oil spills have the potential to affect the health of M. niger in many areas of the Amazon. Additionally, gold mining can involve the destruction of habitats and the disruption of natural water flows. Oil spills are another significant threat to the health of M. niger as they reduce the availability of prey and contaminate the water (Kimerling 1990, Whale 1995, Kimerling 2013, Fraser 2016, Ortiz et al. 2020).

Unregulated tourist activities involving caimans have become increasingly widespread in the Amazon. Ecotourism operations often rely on close human interaction, which can elevate stress hormone levels in M. niger. There is a lack of regulation for operators to adhere to, which means that these activities could negatively impact the health of these animals (Mendonça et al. 2023).
documentation.measures:
Until the 1990s, M. niger was considered one of the most threatened Neotropical crocodilians. The main conservation problems were related to unsustainable use, transformation and habitat loss, and hunting by local fishermen due to alleged competition for resources. With the development and implementation of conservation strategies in the Amazon, the creation of protected areas, and advances in basic research and monitoring programs, the conservation status of this species has been reversed. The identification of high-density populations throughout its distribution indicates that M. niger is an abundant species, only partially and locally depleted (Rebêlo and Magnusson 1983, Yamashita et al. 1996, Da Silveira et al. 1997, Thorbjarnarson 1998, Da Silveira and Thorbjarnarson 1999, Thorbjarnarson 1999, Thorbjarnarson and Da Silveira 2000, Da Silveira 2002, Da Silveira 2003, Da Silveira 2011, Farias et al. 2004, Thorbjarnarson 2010, Botero-Arias et al. 2022).

Although M. niger are considered as Least Concern, the conservation priorities vary between the range states. Conservation priorities are mainly based on the data obtained in Brazil and generalized for the rest of the distribution. Many countries have defined the species conservation status, but without clear measures and information on the population, which makes difficult the implementation of a regional strategy for the conservation of the species.

In the 1970s, the hunting of caimans in South America was banned under federal law. After this prohibition, M. niger populations have increased in many locations. However, the use of caiman meat emerged as an alternative, but illegal, source of food for local people. In more than half of the countries where it is found, natural populations of M. niger are considered to be seriously diminished but their stronghold in Brazil shows a large, widespread and stable population. In Ecuador, Bolivia and Guyana, stable populations, isolated from human settlements, have been documented (Plotkin et al. 1983a, Thorbjarnarson 1999, Thorbjarnarson 2010).

In the 1990s, structured and systematic research efforts were developed on the biology and population dynamics of caiman in the middle Amazon River (known as the Solimões River in Brazil) region. The results of these surveys indicated high abundances of M. niger and Caiman crocodilus with a tendency for the populations to recover quickly after extensive hunting (Da Silveira and Thorbjarnarson 1999).

Overall, M. niger management programs primarily target the protection of natural populations. However, the programs in Ecuador and Brazil have included a sustainable use approach. In Ecuador, a ranching program was implemented with a zero quota for commercial purposes under the CITES Ranching Resolution (Resolution Conf. 11.16) in 1994 but the program was unsuccessful and closed in 2008. In Brazil, M. niger was changed from CITES Appendix I to Appendix II in 2007 and both the state and federal Governments committed themselves to implementing harvest programs for wild populations in Sustainable Development Reserves (Botero-Arias et al. 2010, 2022; Marioni et al. 2021). Unfortunately, the lack of logistical and technical planning, combined with poor biological information to regulate the extraction and sale of caiman products, has aroused strong doubts about the development and future of caiman harvesting programs in the Amazon. The lack of studies on the potential production as well as value chain and marketing strategies based on the historical and cultural context of traditional caiman hunting has limited the potential use of Amazonian caimans (Marioni et al. 2021, Botero-Arias et al. 2022).

The increase in abundance of M. niger was determined by the decrease in the international skin trade in the 1970s combined with the implementation and regulation of the Protected Areas system. However, the illegal meat trade on a regional scale, and using caiman meat as bait in piracatinga fishing, requires special attention to avoid conservation threats to the species. There is a need for the development of a M. niger harvesting system, determined via a strategic conservation plan for all countries involved that includes additional income for Amazonian communities (Marioni et al. 2007, Marioni 2013a; Mendonça et al. 2016; Marioni 2021, Botero-Arias et al. 2022).

Melanosuchus niger conservation strategies would possibly benefit from the definition of criteria for a large-scale population monitoring program. Improved knowledge about biology, breeding ecology and population dynamics could improve decision-making processes for conservation. However, such activities do not substitute for the involvement of local people in habitat protection and sustainable use. This requires understanding of the illegal value chains historically used in local and regional contexts for the M. niger trade (Villamarín et al. 2011, Marioni et al. 2013a, Marioni 2021, Botero-Arias et al. 2022, Esbach et al. 2022).
documentation.use_trade:
Reports from explorers and naturalists indicate that M. niger was abundant in the 19th century (Bates 1863, Fittkau 1970, Smith 1981, Best 1984). Commercial exploitation of the species began at the beginning of the 1900s as a response to the high demand for exotic skins in North America, Europe and Asia (Medem 1981, Brazaitis et al. 1996, Yamashita et al. 1996, Antunes et al. 2016, Mendonça et al. 2016, Marioni et al. 2021, Botero-Arias et al. 2022). The overexploitation of Crocodylus intermedius and C. acutus for the hide market in South America led to a significant decline in their populations and, as a consequence, the trade extended to M. niger as an alternative. Compared to other Amazonian caimans, M. niger was preferred because its skin has less osteoderms which affects the aesthetic appeal of the finished leather (Medem 1971, 1981; Plotkin et al. 1983a; Herron 1985; Brazaitis et al. 1996; Thorbjarnarson 2010).

The harvesting and international trade of M. niger was one of the longest, most widespread, and most intensive of all caiman species in Central and South America. From 1950 to 1965, over 7.5 million legally sourced M. niger skins were supplied to the international market from the Amazon (Medem 1981, Smith 1981, Plotkin et al. 1983a, Da Silveira and Thorbjarnarson 1999, Thorbjarnarson 2010, Antunes et al. 2016, Campos-Silva et al. 2017). There appears to be a relationship between the collapse in 1912 of Amazonian rubber prices and the massive harvesting of M. niger in the central-western Brazilian Amazon. Between 1904 and 1969, 4.4 million M. niger skins were traded from this region. The historical peak was in 1943 when 313,907 were sold. In the 1960s, the number of caimans traded was only 8% of the peak production in 1943 (Antunes et al. 2016).

The commercial exploitation of M. niger finished with the collapse of worldwide skin trade, the intensification of regional enforcement, international regulation of the use and trade of biodiversity, as well as the creation of a system of protected areas and other conservation strategies. However, following the collapse of the skin trade, a well-structured illegal market emerged for M. niger meat. This practice still occurs in several regions of the Amazon and represents a critical threat to the conservation of caimans in some localities (Da Silveira and Thorbjarnarson 1999; Da Silveira 2002, 2003; Marioni et al. 2007; Morales-Betancourt and Trujillo 2015; Mendonça et al. 2016). Over the last 50 years, the intense exploitation of caimans to supply the salted meat market has generated a stable value chain of hunting, processing and trade. Despite being illegal, this dried-salted meat production represents a robust, economical alternative for the local communities many of which are socioeconomically disadvantaged (Botero-Arias et al. 2022).

The use of M. niger as bait for Piracatinga Catfish (Calophysus macropterus) emerged in 2000 as another commercial activity (Da Silveira and Viana 2003). Reports indicate that fishing for this species using caiman baits was implemented initially in Colombia and Peru and introduced in Brazil in 2000, encouraging seasonal trade to supply fish markets during the Catholic Holy Week. The primary concern for piracatinga fishing is not the exploitation of the fish itself but the illegal use of baits made with caiman or dolphin (Inia geoffrensis and Sotalia fluviatilis) meat (Botero-Arias and Regatieri 2013, Botero-Arias et al. 2014, Brum et al. 2015, Franco et al. 2016, Pimenta et al. 2018, Botero-Arias et al. 2022).

The use of caimans and river dolphins as bait for piracatinga fishing has given rise to a lucrative illegal activity, creating a complex underground network of natural-resource exploitation that thrives on inadequate control and enforcement. Studies on the value chain of piracatinga fishing in Brazil have revealed that the originally seasonal activity has become a more frequent source of income for communities due to its accessibility. However, the gradual increase in fishing pressure on aquatic fauna used as bait has raised concerns among scientists, leading to a federal moratorium on piracatinga fishing (Inter-Ministerial Normative Instruction No. 6 of July 17, 2014), which banned the activity for five years, aimed at discouraging the use of crocodilians and dolphins. This moratorium has been renewed in subsequent years until 2023. In July of 2023, the ban was extended indefinitely. However, if sustainable alternatives are identified, piracatinga fishing using alternative baits could be re-evaluated within the next three years. Similar measures have been implemented in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, and efforts have been made to promote sustainable fishing practices, such as using artificial baits and developing alternative livelihoods including ecotourism. Moreover, initiatives have been taken to regulate regional and international piracatinga trade (Da Silveira and Viana 2003, Da Silveira 2011, Botero-Arias et al. 2014, Brum et al. 2015, Franco et al. 2016, Marioni et al. 2021, Botero-Arias et al. 2022).

After reports showed M. niger recovery following a reduction in illegal trade, management programs were proposed to protect the wild populations in Ecuador and Brazil. In Ecuador, a ranching program was implemented with a zero quota for commercial purposes after the species was downlisted in CITES from Appendix I to Appendix II. However, the program was unsuccessful and closed in 2008 due to the need for more value-chain development (Larriera et al. 2005, Velasco 2005). In the Brazilian Amazon, attempts to use M. niger and Caiman crocodilus in ranching systems have similarly been unsuccessful to date (Botero-Arias et al. 2022).

In Brazil, scientific research conducted in the 1990s showed that protection measures had led to a recovery in M. niger populations. The study suggested that a regulated harvest program could be successful based on biological criteria and community co-management. As a result, the state and federal governments committed to implementing harvest programs for wild populations in the Protected Area System, which is allowed and regulated by Brazilian environmental law. In 2007, the listing of M. niger in CITES was changed from Appendix I to Appendix II.

The first experiments involving M. niger were conducted in the Mamirauá SDR in 2004, extracting 61 individuals. Subsequently, two additional harvests were carried out in 2006 and 2008, with the removal of 567 individuals. These three events were led by the state of Amazonas Government, with the primary objective of validating slaughtering and processing techniques with the focus on improving the sanitary aspects of meat production, including defining technical criteria for slaughtering and pre-processing the meat while identifying critical contamination points throughout the process (Botero-Arias et al. 2009, Botero-Arias and Regatieri 2014). Similar harvesting activities for M. niger and Caiman crocodilus have been developed in the Lake of Cuniã Extractive Reserve (RESEX), in the State of Rondônia (Marioni et al. 2021, Botero-Arias et al. 2022).

The commercial expectation of the harvesting system in Brazil was that meat was to be sold on local markets, and the skins would be primarily supplied to the domestic leather industry. Between 2008 and 2018, Brazil exported 2,272 M. niger skins, mainly to Mexico and Argentina, as well as a much smaller number to European and Asian markets.

In 2011, a legal framework supported by the state of the Amazonas for the local indigenous use of M. niger meat included specific technical guidelines for harvesting, slaughtering and processing. It was not until 2020, nine years after the latest regulations were enacted, that another commercial offtake of crocodilians was carried out in Mamirauá SDR. On this occasion, 28 M. niger were harvested and processed on a floating structure. The resulting products were sold locally, while the skins were sold to a private enterprise in another Brazilian state for further testing of processing technologies (Franco 2021). Although the commercial harvest was deemed successful, the high investment required for constructing, maintaining and operating the processing structure, coupled with limited information on the value chain, makes replicating this experience in other Amazonian locations challenging (Marioni et al. 2021, Botero-Arias et al. 2022).

Melanosuchus niger trade is carried out illegally in a diffuse manner, with a primary focus on marketing in urban areas. The skin is discarded due to gaps in the trade, processing and value chain. Despite efforts to explore sustainable use through experimental programs, a straightforward, comprehensive management approach has yet to be established for this species. As a result, the current state of M. niger management remains experimental, and there is a need for more effective measures to ensure that it is sustainably utilized in a way that benefits both local communities and the broader ecosystem (Botero-Arias et al. 2010, Botero-Arias and Regatieri 2013, Marioni et al. 2013, Franco et al. 2019, Marioni et al. 2021, Silva et al. 2021, Botero-Arias et al. 2010).

Ecotourism activities involving interaction with free-living caimans have been the only non-consumptive-use option for the Amazonian species. This economic activity occurs throughout the Amazon and represents an important source of income for local people. However, it is still largely unregulated, and the actual impact both economically and on the caimans themselves is poorly understood. Wildlife tourism is increasingly seen as an economically viable option for justifying conservation efforts to protect large predators.

In Guyana, since the early 2000s, M. niger has been incorporated as a monetary incentive in wildlife tourism activities, offering local communities a significant source of income. This initiative not only provides economic benefits but also has positively influenced the attitudes of the local community in Yupukari towards wildlife conservation. M. niger tourism has become an effective and sustainable economic alternative that undergoes continual evaluation and improvement (Spellen 2019, Rosenblatt et al. 2021).

Experimental research has recently been conducted at two sites in the Brazilian Amazon with differing environmental characteristics (varzea and igapo) to evaluate the level of physiological stress experienced by individuals during human-crocodilian interactions in tourism activities. Results from the study suggest that M. niger individuals experience more intense stress-related physiological reactions from manipulation and flash photography than sympatric individuals of Caiman crocodilus (Mendonça et al. 2023). Melanosuchus niger took over 6 hours to return to basal-range corticosterone levels after muscular stress, whereas Caiman crocodilus only took half an hour (Duncan et al. 2022). This research aims to provide information that can be used to develop safe public policies.
documentation.rationale:
Black Caiman (Melanosuchus niger) has a wide distribution across northern and central South America. Although this species was heavily exploited during the mid-20th century, populations have recovered considerably, and healthy populations thrive throughout much of the species’ range. Population reduction over the last three generations (75 years) has been estimated as less than 30% and thus does not qualify the species as threatened under criterion A.

Both its extent of occurrence (EOO) and area of occupancy (AOO) are well above the thresholds, therefore it does not qualify as threatened under criterion B. Similarly, the estimated number of mature individuals is approximately 10,000, thus exceeding the thresholds of both criteria C and D. No quantitative analysis on probability of extinction has been conducted, therefore criterion E cannot be applied.

Based on the above, and the lack of change in the population since the last assessment in 2000, Melanosuchus niger is assessed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
The genus Melanosuchus has been reported in the late Miocene in South America (De Souza-Filho et al. 2020), and the Black Caiman is the only living species of this genus (Medina 1976; Brochu 1999; Oaks 2011; Bona et al. 2014, 2017; Foth et al. 2015; De Souza-Filho et al. 2020; Rio and Mannion 2021). No subspecies are recognized.

In morphology-based phylogenetic analyses, Melanosuchus appears within the genus Caiman and, in some cases, as the sister clade of Caiman latirostris (Poe 1996, Brochu 1999, Salas-Gismondi et al. 2015, Hastings et al. 2016), which led to the proposal that Melanosuchus niger should be assigned to the genus Caiman (Poe 1996). However, phylogenies recovered from molecular data strongly support the monophyly of the genus Caiman and place Melanosuchus niger as a sister species of this group (Hrbek et al. 2008, Oaks 2011, Bittencourt et al. 2019, Roberto et al. 2020, Muniz et al. 2021) and is recognised by the IUCN SSC Crocodile Specialist Group Taxonomy and Identification Group (Vliet et al. 2024).
